title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
coram: S. Abdul Nazeer & Krishna Murari, JJ. (delivered by S. Abdul Nazeer, J.)
docket: Civil Appeal No. 4324 of 2015 (with C.A. No. 4323 of 2015)
disposition: Appeals allowed in part (DERC/APTEL findings on Issues 1-6 set aside to the stated extent)
headnote: A tariff order made under Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is quasi-judicial and binding until amended or revoked under Section 64(6); at the 'truing up' stage the Regulator cannot 'change the rules of the game after it has begun' by altering the methodology/principles of the initial determination, which would be an impermissible retrospective revision of tariff. Separately, on enforcement (theft/unauthorised-use) sales: where the Supply Code Regulations and Section 126 create a legal fiction that assessed energy is 'deemed' consumed/sold, that fiction must be carried to its logical end — the assessed units must be treated as 'sales', notwithstanding a Lok Adalat settlement reducing only the rupee amount.

holding_units.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination
holding_units.question: May a State Commission, at the 'truing up' stage, change the methodology or principles used in the initial tariff determination, or otherwise retrospectively amend a tariff order?
holding_units.holding: No. A tariff order under s.64 is quasi-judicial and binding until amended/revoked under s.64(6); truing up is only the adjustment of actuals against projections and cannot be used to re-think de novo the basic principles or retrospectively change the methodology of the initial determination. The DERC's changes on Issues 1, 2, 3 and 5 (LPSC/collection efficiency, depreciation, FR/SR salary, fringe benefit tax) were impermissible and are set aside; interest on Consumer Security Deposit (Issue 4) is a legitimate expense the appellants may recover.

holding_units.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with the DERC Supply Code Regulations)
holding_units.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect
holding_units.question: In enforcement (theft/unauthorised-use) cases, must energy 'deemed' consumed under the Supply Code Regulations and Section 126 be treated as 'sales' for AT&C-loss computation, even where a Lok Adalat settlement reduces only the rupee amount recovered?
holding_units.holding: Yes. Where the statute and the DERC Supply Code Regulations create a legal fiction that assessed energy is 'deemed' consumed (e.g. under the LDHF formula), the fiction must be taken to its logical end: the assessed units must be treated as 'sales'. The DERC's method of back-calculating units from the reduced settlement amount is contrary to law; assessed energy is to be considered as supply, with the impact and carrying costs allowed.

principle_tags.application: A Regulator cannot, at the truing-up stage, change the methodology or principles of the initial tariff determination; doing so is an impermissible retrospective revision of a quasi-judicial tariff order.
When the Supply Code / Section 126 deems assessed energy to be consumed, the fiction must be given full effect and the assessed units treated as sales.

not_decided.point: Remaining substantial questions on Issues 1-3, 5 and 6
not_decided.note: Having set aside the truing-up changes, the Court found it unnecessary to answer the other substantial questions of law framed on those issues, and likewise the other contentions on Issue 6.

authorities.name: Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd.
authorities.proposition: Test for a 'substantial question of law': one of general public importance or directly and substantially affecting the parties' rights, not finally settled or free from difficulty.
authorities.how_treated: Relied on to frame the s.125 substantial-question-of-law threshold.

authorities.name: PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
authorities.proposition: Tariff fixation under Section 62 is quasi-judicial (and appealable under s.111), while Section 61 is the enabling provision for framing generic regulations.
authorities.how_treated: Relied on for the quasi-judicial character of tariff determination.

authorities.name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Tarini Infrastructure Ltd.
authorities.proposition: Tariff incorporated in a power purchase agreement is not a pure act of volition alterable only by mutual consent.
authorities.how_treated: Distinguished — held not applicable to the present (non-contractual, truing-up) facts.

authorities.name: State Load Despatch Centre v. GERC
authorities.proposition: 'Truing up' means the adjustment of actual amounts incurred against the estimated/projected amounts determined under the ARR.

authorities.name: North Delhi Power Ltd. (NDPL) v. DERC
authorities.proposition: Restricting a utility's claim by disallowing reasonably anticipated expenditure and deferring it to the truing-up exercise is not prudence; truing up only fills the gap between actual and anticipated expenses.
